title: Entitlement disclaimers and discretion-constraining statutes
summary: A no-entitlement label raises an interpretive question distinct from whether operative law actually secures a benefit and limits administrative discretion.
notes:
The notes ask whether a legislature can prescribe mandatory eligibility conditions yet disclaim the creation of constitutional property. Washington Legal Clinic for the Homeless v. Barry treated the operative limits on discretion as central, but found none sufficient in the shelter laws; the editors accordingly caution that its rejection of the disclaimer argument may be dictum.

Weston v. Cassata involved Colorado welfare recipients challenging sanction notices. The court read the state program’s mandatory grant language, continuation during appeal, and notice protections as eliminating discretion to deny assistance to persons meeting the specified criteria. It construed the federal no-entitlement language with attention to conditional federal block grants and the absence of an unconditional individual guarantee. The opinion adopted Cynthia Farina’s distinction: legislatures choose substantive conditions, while courts determine whether the resulting legal interest receives constitutional protection.

The reading also raises reliance under DACA and describes welfare administration’s shift toward individualized responsibility agreements, sanctions, performance measures, and caseworker discretion. Those examples underscore the need to examine operative text and program structure rather than infer either entitlement or its absence from a program’s title.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: Substantive criteria and disclaimers require contextual construction; legislative labels do not automatically answer whether constitutional property exists.
